author: George Kazamias
headline: Chief Investment Strategist at GCK Global Investments
text:
What happens when a diplomat's private fund is financed by the governments across the table?

That question is driving a growing congressional inquiry into #Affinity Partners, the private equity firm founded by Jared Kushner.

On the record:

• Saudi Arabia's  🇸🇦 Public Investment Fund #PIF committed $2 #billion in 2021a few months after his father in law left the White House.

• Foreign-sourced funds rose from about $3 billion to $4.8 billion during 2024, per an SEC filing cited by lawmakers.

• House Judiciary Democrats now put assets near $6.16 billion, 99% foreign-funded.

• Mr. Kushner has also held a public role on Middle East, Gaza, Iran and Ukraine policy as a special envoy of his father in law and was praised by his father in law for his role in achieving the Abraham Accords.

• In March 2026, Rep. Garcia and Sen. Wyden asked Affinity and the White House about foreign-government contacts, #fundraising and #conflict safeguards. More letters followed in April, October and November

The fee figures cited are congressional estimates and allegations, not findings of illegal payments. The letters come from minority Democrats. Affinity says it held only early-stage fundraising talks, and the White House says Mr. Kushner acts in the public's interest.

Why it matters:

1. Perceived conflicts erode trust, even absent wrongdoing.

2. Disclosure and vetting rules may not fit informal envoy roles.

3. Anyone handling sovereign capital should expect tougher governance scrutiny.

author: Ali A.
headline: Senior Project Manager| Head of Business I Fit-Out & Construction | MEP I ELV | PMP®
text:
ALEC spent 26 years as a private contractor in Dubai. When the Investment Corporation of Dubai sold 20 percent of it on the DFM in October 2025, the offer was covered more than 21 times.

The numbers investors were buying deserve a slow read. Revenue of AED 8.1 billion in 2024. EBITDA margin around 8 percent. Net margin around 4 percent. Roughly four fils of profit on every dirham of work. Nobody in contracting gets rich on that line alone.

What the market paid for was the shape of the record. Management says the business has been profitable for 18 straight years, with one softer year in 2017 linked to its work in Qatar. Most contractors in this region cannot show five clean years in a row, never mind eighteen.

The backlog helped too, AED 35.4 billion at mid-2025. But 79 percent of it was won in the previous two years, and 13 percent sits in Saudi. The history was earned in the UAE. A growing share of the future gets delivered in Riyadh.

That is the part I would watch. Saudi labour costs, Saudi payment cycles, long truck runs from Jeddah. Can an 8 percent business stay an 8 percent business across the border?

If you are underwriting a contractor in the Kingdom, the lesson is simple. A thin margin held for a long time is worth more than a fat one held for three good years.

Which Saudi contractor could show you 18 years without a loss?

#Investing #Contracting #GCC

text:
Saudi Arabia deployed SR34.51 billion into R&D in 2025. Up 17% year-on-year. Employment in the sector climbed 20% to 67,691.

The researcher count hit 49,383. Up 19% from 2024.

Business accounts for 44.8% of total R&D spend. Government at 37.5%. Higher education at 17.7%.

The surprise: large entities drove 97.9% of total expenditure. Micro, small, and medium-sized entities contributed just 2.1%.

R&D as a share of GDP reached 0.72% in 2025.

The Kingdom is building innovation capacity at scale. The investment split between business and government is real. The constraint is not capital or commitment.

The constraint is talent density in the mid-tier and startup layers. 2.1% of spend from small and medium entities signals a narrow base.

Vision 2030 runs on research infrastructure. Broad participation matters as much as absolute spend.

Worth watching if you are tracking Saudi capability buildout.

via Saudi Gazette

text:
Raising from an angel investor is a major milestone.Doing it on a handshake is one of the fastest ways to break your cap table.
Moving a startup from MVP to scale takes more than capital—it requires a tight legal roadmap that protects both founders and investors before a single Riyal changes hands.
Here are the 5 legal stages every Saudi startup needs to navigate when onboarding an angel investor:

1. Negotiation & Alignment Before sharing sensitive financials or code, lock in the basics: 
• NDA to protect confidential business data. 
• LOI or Term Sheet to align on valuation, equity, and core deal terms before spending time on long-form contracts.

2. Due Diligence Expect the investor’s legal and financial advisors to look under the hood. They will verify your Commercial Registration (CR), licenses, Articles of Association (AoA), intellectual property ownership, and any hidden legal liabilities.

3. Choosing the Investment Instrument How the money enters the company matters just as much as the amount: 
• Direct Equity: Immediate shares in exchange for capital + amending the AoA. (Crucial: clarify whether funds are Cash-in to grow the company, or Cash-out paid to founders for transferring existing shares.) 
• Convertible Notes: Debt that converts into equity in a future round, usually at a discount. 
• SAFE Agreement: A flexible startup standard granting future equity without forcing an immediate valuation.

text:
Before committing to an AI partnership, I would want to understand how the first paid deployment will happen.

An institution may have a business unit willing to fund a deployment, access to relevant data, and customers who could use the service. A technology partner may have a working capability and need sector expertise, local integration and a route to those customers.

The partnership has to make those contributions commercially workable.

For a CAIO or CDO evaluating that arrangement, I would put three decisions into the agreement early. Who owns the customer relationship? Who is accountable for the service after deployment? How will the parties share delivery costs and revenue?

Those answers affect which partner I would bring into the conversation and what I would ask each side to commit to.

As I explore opportunities across AI, data and fintech, I’m interested in connecting with institutions in Qatar and the wider GCC that have a defined requirement and are looking for the right technology partnership.

Janus Henderson plans a final close on a US$300 million fund early next year, Sikander Ahmed, its head of MENA private credit, said, and Benefit Street Partners chief executive David Manlowe, whose Franklin Templeton-owned firm manages about US$97 billion, expects the Middle East to become one of the world's largest private credit markets over the next five to 10 years.

author: Ronald Achs
headline: Founder at Oil-Royalties.com
text:
A royalty check tells you what a well paid last month. It doesn't necessarily tell you what the underlying mineral interest is worth.

Consider two producing oil wells generating similar royalty payments today. One may have a long, relatively stable production history. The other may be experiencing a steep decline after an unusually productive first year.

The checks look similar. The future income streams may be very different.

For royalty owners considering a sale, understanding production decline, commodity-price exposure, ownership decimals, and the remaining economic life of the wells can make a substantial difference in evaluating an offer.

And there is an important distinction: royalty owners never pay the wells' drilling, completion, or operating expenses. Working interest owners, by contrast, bear their contractual share of those costs and associated obligations.

That's why a buyer's valuation should reflect the actual interest being acquired.

Max-Bid Value™ (MBV) provides a framework for establishing an acquisition price ceiling based on projected economics. Cash Flow Model (CFM) allows users to examine how changing assumptions affect projected cash flow over time.

The Middle East Investor Brief ☕ 

𝗠𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗹𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 £𝟰𝟯𝗯𝗻 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁. 

Mubadala and Centerbridge have agreed to acquire Canaccord Wealth at an enterprise value of about £1.17bn. Gulf sovereign capital is now buying the distribution of wealth management in mature markets, not just allocating through it. 

It was a heavy week for that trade in both directions. Blackstone opened a private wealth office in the DIFC and upgraded its ADGM licence. Morrison and Heitman both planted flags in Abu Dhabi. Goldman Sachs, Fortress and HSBC closed the largest Saudi private credit deal since February, alongside regional managers Ruya and Amwal. 

Bankers at Zawya's forum on Wednesday set out the recovery: bonds and sukuk in January, listings from the second quarter, with Citi working on three IPOs in the UAE and three in Saudi Arabia. Both conditions were stated plainly. The region stays calm, and sellers accept lower valuations than they got before the war. 

𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸'𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗳: 
🏦 Mubadala and Centerbridge to buy Canaccord Wealth at a £1.17bn enterprise value 
📅 Gulf bankers see bonds in January and IPOs from Q2, if the region stays calm 
💰 Goldman, Fortress and HSBC back a $150m Saudi private credit financing 
💼 Blackstone opens a DIFC private wealth office, Kuwait next 
🏢 Morrison and Heitman add $84bn of managed assets to the ADGM roster 
📱 iMENA raises SAR 802m privately while it waits for the listing window
